e.etymology: From Old French Josse, the name of a 7th-century Breton saint, Iodoc, from a Breton word for lord. It was a men's name in the Middle Ages; its later use for girls owes much to its likeness to joy and rejoice.
namesakes: Joyce Carol Oates (novelist)
Joyce Meyer (televangelist and author)
Joyce Byers (Winona Ryder's character in Stranger Things)

assoc.t: James Joyce, Irish author of Ulysses

e.etymology: A respelling of Colton, an English surname from a place name, Old English for the settlement of a man named Cola.

e.meaning: first, primordial; a name of the goddess Durga
e.etymology: From Sanskrit adya, first or original. Adya Shakti, the primal power, is a title of the goddess Durga, which gives the name its religious weight.
The English form of Irish Breandan, Old Irish Brenainn, from an Old Welsh word for prince or king. Saint Brendan the Navigator, a 6th-century Irish abbot, is famous for his legendary Atlantic voyage.
namesakes: Brendan Fraser (actor, The Mummy and The Whale)
Brendan Gleeson (Irish actor)
Saint Brendan the Navigator (6th-century Irish abbot)

e.etymology: The English spelling of Scottish Gaelic Alasdair, the Gaelic form of Alexander, from Greek alexein, to defend, and aner, man.
namesakes: Alistair Cooke (journalist and host of Masterpiece Theatre)

e.meaning: firm, enduring, as a form of Ethan
e.etymology: A Spanish spelling of the way Ethan sounds in English, popular in Spain since the 2000s. It also matches the Basque verb izan, to be, and a name Izani appears in a 10th-century Basque record.
From Hebrew ze'ev, wolf. In Jewish tradition the wolf is the emblem of the tribe of Benjamin, and Zev is often paired with the Yiddish name Wolf.
The Greek form of the Hebrew name Uzziah, the Lord is my strength. King Uzziah of Judah is called Ozias in the King James New Testament.
From Italian Salvatore, Latin salvator, savior, given in honor of Christ as the Savior. It is especially common in Sicily and southern Italy; Salvador is the Spanish form.
namesakes: Salvatore Ferragamo (Italian shoe designer)

e.meaning: little king (the traditional reading of Irish Rian)
e.etymology: A spelling of Ryan used mostly for girls. Ryan is from the Irish surname O Riain, descendant of Rian, a name usually explained as little king.
The English name of the blue gem, from Greek sappheiros, a word that reaches back to Hebrew sappir. It joins Ruby, Pearl and Jade among the jewel names.

assoc.t: sapphire, the blue gem and September birthstone
Bombay Sapphire gin, often ordered as Sapphire

e.note: Sapphire is also the name of an old stereotype of Black women as angry and overbearing, from a character on Amos 'n' Andy.

e.etymology: Made known by model and fashion designer Kimora Lee Simmons, whose fame from the late 1990s put the name on American charts. Its roots beyond that are not established.
namesakes: Kimora Lee Simmons (model and fashion designer)

assoc.t: Kimora Lee Simmons, model and Baby Phat designer

e.etymology: From the Cornish word elowen, elm tree. It came into use as a given name in Cornwall in the 20th century, as part of the revival of the Cornish language.
From French belle, beautiful, from Latin bella. It is also a short form of Isabelle, Annabelle and other names with that ending.
namesakes: Belle (heroine of Disney's Beauty and the Beast)
Belle Starr (Wild West outlaw)

assoc.t: Belle of Disney's Beauty and the Beast
belle of the ball; Southern belle

e.meaning: lisping (the usual reading of Latin Blasius)
e.etymology: The French form of Latin Blasius, usually traced to blaesus, lisping. Saint Blaise was a 4th-century Armenian bishop, and the name is also known from the French mathematician Blaise Pascal.
namesakes: Blaise Pascal (17th-century French mathematician and philosopher)
e.note: Sounds the same as blaze, the word for a fire.

e.meaning: pet form of Benjamin (son of the right hand)
e.etymology: A pet form of Benjamin, from Hebrew Binyamin, son of the right hand, and less often of Benedict or Bennett. It has long been given as a full name.
namesakes: Benny Goodman (bandleader, the King of Swing)
Benny Hill (British comedian)
Benny Blanco (record producer)

e.etymology: The Yiddish form of Israel, from Hebrew Yisrael, the name Jacob received after wrestling with the angel in Genesis. It is used chiefly in Orthodox Jewish families.
A modern American coinage, most likely a blend of Aubrey and Gabrielle.
The English word rain used as a name, in the same spirit as River and Sky. In Estonia Rain is a separate men's name, short for Rainer.

assoc.t: Rain, the South Korean pop singer and actor

e.etymology: A form of the English surname Colson, son of Cole, where Cole was a medieval short form of Nicholas. This spelling keeps the name Cole visible.
Brought to notice by rapper Kevin Gates, who gave the name to his son and to his 2022 album Khaza. Its origin beyond that is not established.

assoc.t: Khaza, 2022 album by rapper Kevin Gates

e.meaning: blessed reconciliation; also read as friend of peace
e.etymology: The English form of Welsh Gwenfrewi, from gwen, white or blessed, and a word for reconciliation, reshaped to match the Old English name Winfrith, friend of peace. Saint Winifred was a 7th-century Welsh martyr.
namesakes: Winifred Sanderson (Bette Midler's witch in Hocus Pocus)
Winifred Banks (the mother in Mary Poppins)

assoc.t: Winifred Sanderson, lead witch of Hocus Pocus

e.etymology: A spelling of Amir, from Arabic amir, commander or prince, the word behind the title emir.

From Late Latin Benedictus, blessed, from bene, well, and dicere, to speak. Saint Benedict of Nursia founded the Benedictine order in the 6th century, and many popes have taken the name, most recently Benedict XVI.
namesakes: Benedict Cumberbatch (actor, Sherlock and Doctor Strange)
Pope Benedict XVI (pope from 2005 to 2013)
Benedict Arnold (Revolutionary War general turned traitor)

assoc.t: Benedict Arnold, byword for a traitor

e.note: In the US, calling someone a Benedict Arnold means calling them a traitor.

e.meaning: shining light, by way of Helen
e.etymology: The medieval English form of Helen, from Greek Helene, a name of uncertain root often linked to a word for torch or bright light. It has also served as a short form of Eleanor.
namesakes: Ellen DeGeneres (comedian and talk show host)
Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver's hero in the Alien films)
Ellen Burstyn (Oscar-winning actress)

assoc.t: Ellen DeGeneres and her talk show, Ellen

e.meaning: heath, open land covered with heather
e.etymology: An English surname for someone who lived on a heath, from Old English haeth, open uncultivated land. It became a first name in the 1900s.
namesakes: Heath Ledger (actor, The Dark Knight)

assoc.t: Heath, the chocolate toffee candy bar
Heath Ledger, actor who played the Joker

e.etymology: In the US mostly a Spanish-influenced spelling of Kaylee or Kayley, used in Latino families. Keily is also an Irish surname, a form of Kiely.
One of many spellings of Kaylee, a modern American name built from Kay and Lee that peaked around 2009.
The feminine form of Carl and Carlo, from the Germanic word karl, free man, the same root as Charles. English speakers borrowed it from German and Italian.
namesakes: Carla Tortelli (the waitress on Cheers)
Carla Gugino (actress)
Carla Bruni (singer and former first lady of France)

e.etymology: A K spelling of Cadence, the English word for rhythm or the fall of the voice, from Latin cadentia, a falling. Cadence became a girls' name in the early 2000s.
A modern American coinage in the pattern of Kyla, Nyla and Ayla with the fashionable Z opening. It is unrelated to the Polish surname spelled the same way.
A 20th-century invention, probably modeled on Darius or Dorian. Darien is the other common spelling.
